items.story_key: model:gemini|ver:4|title:introducing gemini 4 neon
items.content_excerpt: Bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Neon — bringing frontier-level intelligence with fast end-to-end task completion across complex software engineering, knowledge work, and science workflows. Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models. On the Vals Index , Neon ranks #2 and lands on the Pareto frontier. Beyond just pushing on raw model capability, we’re continuing to make our models better to work with, Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index . Neon also excels at multi-step instruction following and builds on our ongoing progress to curb fabrication, recording our lowest fabrication rate yet in internal Google Antigravity testing. The model is priced at $3 per million input tokens ($0.15 per million cached input tokens, a 95% discount) and $15 per million output tokens, with a 1 million-token context window. Gemini 4 Neon is rolling out today in the Gemini API in Google AI Studio , Gemini for business (via API and model dropdown), for paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity , and for Pro and Ultra subscribers in the Gemini app . Enterprise work lives in spreadsheets, PDFs, charts, audio, and video. Neon can synthesize across all of these inputs in a single 1 million-token context window and turns inputs into structured deliverables. Independent evaluations rank Neon as one of the top models and on benchmarks like the Vals Index , it ranks #2 (70.9%), and reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench . Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI , ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts and performs on par with leading models on Agents' Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs' Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. items.title: KnowledgeClaw: Towards Agentic Knowledge Engineering via Omnimodal Hypergraphs
items.summary: Knowledge engineering (KE) turns raw files into a reasoning-ready knowledge base, a task now within reach of LLM agents. KE has progressed from chunk and graph retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to memory agents, agentic KE and multimodal KE. However, a live knowledge base needs omnimodality, a closed-loop lifecycle and multi-granular application at once, yet existing systems meet at most two and no benchmark measures all three. We formalize Omnimodal Knowledge Engineering (OmniKE) and release OmniKE-Bench, six tasks with 1,829 model-free items over 3,960 real files in five modalities. We further propose KnowledgeClaw, an agentic system that builds an omnimodal typed hypergraph, keeps it current with a closed-loop lifecycle agent and routes each query to the granularity it needs. Against 30 baselines, it ranks first on all six tasks with an overall OKE of 55.9, +14.6 over the strongest baseline. Our software and data are publicly available at https://github.com/LHRLAB/KnowledgeClaw.

items.title: DaisyRose-27B: Pushing the Frontier of Post-Training Efficiency
items.story_key: story|ver:27|title:daisyrose 27b pushing the frontier of post training efficiency
items.content_excerpt: Today we are releasing DaisyRose-27B , RadixArk’s first model, built on Qwen3.8-27B and trained with reinforcement learning using Miles . We trained it on long-horizon agent tasks with sessions up to 1M tokens, with just 1,200 curated tasks in 18 days on 144 H200 GPUs. DaisyRose-27B improves Terminal-Bench 4.1 pass@1 from 5.6% to 12.0% . Beyond Terminal-Bench 4.1, it also delivers gains on a variety of other reasoning, instruction following, and coding benchmarks. The model retains Qwen3.8-27B’s architecture, tokenizer, chat template, image understanding, and 256K-token context window . The longer training sessions use harness summarization to span multiple trajectories. See the model card for model properties and inference settings. We recommend serving DaisyRose-27B with SGLang and DSpark speculative decoding. The SGLang cookbook provides launch configurations for different GPUs and checkpoint formats. After starting the server with the served model name DaisyRose-27B on port 30000 , you can send a request using the OpenAI Python client: The model thinks before answering by default. Its reasoning is returned in reasoning_content , and its final answer in content . These settings follow the model card’s quickstart . DaisyRose-27B scores higher than the original Qwen3.8-27B model on every benchmark above. The largest gain is on Terminal Bench 4.1, where pass@1 rises from 5.6% to 12.0%. Scores use the higher of the BF16 and FP8 runs for each benchmark; the two differ by less than one point wherever both were evaluated. The model card includes comparison sources and evaluation settings. Three parts of the training setup made this release possible: carefully designed tasks, an efficient training backend, and reliable sandboxes. We built the tasks in partnership with Eigent AI , starting from its large pool of tasks in machine learning, software engineering, science, and other fields. Together we built thousands of candidates. About 1,200 made it into the final training set. RadixArk trained DaisyRose-27B with Miles, our open-source reinforcement learning framework for large-scale model post-training, in fully asynchronous mode: the agent keeps working while the model learns, and neither waits for the other. While 128 H200s run the inference on agent tasks, 16 more run the trainer and learn from the trajectories. After every step, the updated model goes out to the 128 GPUs that run the agent. items.title: QDA: Closed-Loop LLM Quantization Design with Agents
items.summary: Post-training quantization is the standard way to serve large language models at low cost. However, the best quantization recipe differs across models and precisions. As a result, experts must redesign it for every new model, which is time-consuming and often sub-optimal. Fortunately, an LLM agent can take over this design by refining the recipe over rounds of building and evaluating candidates, so that more rounds lead to better recipes. However, evaluating one quantized reasoning model takes tens of GPU-hours, and combining methods from different codebases means porting each to the new architecture by hand. We present QDA, a system in which an agent designs the recipe for each model and precision. To make evaluation fast, QDA scores each candidate in minutes by its output KL divergence from the original model on reasoning traces that the agent never sees, and checks promising ones with long generations to catch failures such as repetition loops. To make building fast, QDA provides a library of public PTQ methods that are compatible with one another and with new model architectures. Across four reasoning models, QDA improves accuracy over the strongest public recipe by 0.9, 1.4 and 2.2 percentage points on average at W4A16, W4A8 and W3A16, using 64 GPU-hours per search. On the 320B-parameter MoE model GLM-5.3-Flash at NVFP4 W4A4, it recovers 98.3% of the FP8 model's accuracy, against 96.9% for the best vendor checkpoint. Every QDA checkpoint also runs on existing serving kernels with no inference overhead. We will release the library, the evaluator and the harness.

items.title: External sandboxes for coding agents
items.summary:
External sandboxes for coding agents

I've been exploring new ways to sandbox code that is executed by agents, with a focus on making it safer to try out local models without worrying that a mistake or prompt injection attack might cause them to take damaging actions on a machine.

I worked on this project with Prime Radiant, the AI research lab behind Superpowers and other projects.

My post on the Prime Radiant blog introduces the external sandbox pattern, where code executed by the agent runs inside a dedicated sandbox while the agent itself lives outside of that sandbox.

To demonstrate this pattern we've released three sandbox server implementations:

  • external-sandbox-v86 runs a Node.js server which then uses v86 to run Alpine Linux inside WebAssembly.
  • external-sandbox-container is a Python web server which runs the sandbox in Alpine Linux inside an Apple Containers instance.
  • external-sandbox-quicksand is another Python web server, this time using Microsoft's Quicksand sandboxing library, which bundles QEMU and Alpine Linux in a Python package!

Each of these implementations offers the same localhost API. You can then configure Pi, Claude Code, or Codex to send API calls to that sandbox any time they want to execute code.

The sandboxes also include an optional HTTP/HTTPS allow-list proxy, so you can control exactly which hosts your agent's code is allowed to communicate with - plus a credential replacement mechanism to make authenticated API calls without sharing a secret with the agent. Here's the UI you can use to reconfigure that proxy while the sandbox is still running:

I continue to be fascinated by the challenge of safely running untrusted code. This external sandbox pattern provides a neat way to experiment with different approaches.

Tags: sandboxing, security, ai, webassembly, generative-ai, llms, coding-agents, claude-code, codex, pi

items.title: How the Claude Code team thinks about verification
items.summary: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest.
items.story_key: model:claude code|title:how the claude code team thinks about verification
items.content_excerpt: How end-to-end, property and differential tests let coding agents verify their work with evidence, and what the Claude Code team does to keep its verifiers honest. On the Claude Code team, the vast majority of our code (~90%) is written and reviewed by Claude . At this scale, how we equip our agents to verify their work with evidence becomes extremely important. Verification loops are the building block that lets you delegate more work to Claude. Without them, you can really only run one or two Claudes at a time, because you have to check everything yourself. With them, you can run dozens or hundreds in parallel. That’s because giving agents a way to verify their output is an effective way to improve quality. In internal testing around structured file generation, having a separate grader check Claude’s work against a rubric improved task success by up to 10 points over a standard prompting loop, with the largest gains on the hardest problems. What was once expensive to verify (tests, benchmarks, specs, real end-to-end runs) is now cheap to request from an agent. Like code, agents can quickly generate tests, benchmarks, and specs. And once generated, these tests and benchmarks run as software so they can be run frequently without using many additional tokens. You can also close the verification loop by using the results to improve the agent’s performance on that task. For example, if an agent repeatedly fails a test that checks logs for user data, you can create a hook or a more explicit rule in your CLAUDE.md to avoid future issues. This (mostly) stops issues from happening again. So if verification is critical to producing quality code at a high velocity, what types of tests should you use and how should you apply them across your pipeline? This article answers those questions and also shares the process used by the Claude Code team. If your tests are flaky you’ll train the agent to run them again rather than fixing the failing code. If your tests are slow, the agent will do fewer tests across batches which can make pinpointing issues difficult. Heavier tests are best deployed before you’ve committed the changes. If you have to focus on one test type, pick end-to-end. These tests describe real user flows like adding an item to a cart, checking out, and moving to a confirmation page. The reason E2E tests are so effective is that they are difficult to fool–either the whole feature works or it doesn't. They also have definitive done criteria and can concrete

items.story_key: story|title:introducing unity gateway insights
items.content_excerpt: When looking to cut AI costs, teams often start with budgets or open-source models. But agent traces can reveal other opportunities to save. At Databricks, trace analysis surfaced several: offline replays showed no performance gain from upgrading from Opus 4.8 to Opus 5, so we stayed on the cheaper 4.8; fixing common MCP errors recovered an estimated $1.2M in costs a year ; and traces showed that simple prompts were going to expensive models, prompting us to adopt Smart Routing . Today, we’re introducing Unity Gateway Insights , which automatically uses Genie to analyze millions of agent traces alongside your business data and ontology. It surfaces where tokens are being wasted: MCP errors that keep recurring, simple tasks running on expensive frontier models, and repeated workflows worth turning into shared skills, all in the context of your business and under the same governance as your other data. If you already have traffic flowing through Unity Gateway, open AI Gateway > Observability > Insights and generate a report for the last day, 7 days, or 30 days. Insights then writes a report on the tokenomics of your coding agent rollout that answers the following questions: You can add up to 10 questions of your own to a report, such as whether the newest model is worth it for your team's work. To dig further, continue the conversation with Genie. Ask which MCP server wasted the most tokens this month and who owns it, and you have a bug report ready to send. Finding this kind of waste requires a full record of every step of every agent session: inputs and outputs, tool calls, subagents, intermediate steps, latency, and token cost. A standalone gateway records only the requests that pass through it. Capturing the rest of each session means instrumenting every coding agent yourself, then exporting the traces to a data platform to analyze them. Pointing Claude Code at those traces still leaves you to design the investigation yourself, with no map of your business like the Genie Ontology provides. Insights runs the investigation we developed while rolling out coding agents to thousands of Databricks engineers. It samples sessions and groups them into workstreams by kind of work. Then it checks each workstream for failing MCP tools, bloated context, frontier models on simple tasks, and repeated workflows, and ranks what it finds by the tokens at stake. items.story_key: story|variant:flash|title:an updated clairic and clairic flash are now open weight from the new workers ai
items.content_excerpt: Cloudflare has become a neolab. We’re building our own frontier AI models for our customers and the open-source community. Both extraction models are hosted on Workers AI and full open weights are available on Hugging Face . We’re also excited to re-introduce ourselves as the Workers AI superintelligence team, the frontier AI research team behind Clef , Clairic, and lots more in the works. This team is working quickly to push the AI frontier and build useful models for Cloudflare’s customers and the open source community. Since announcing Clairic in preview, we have received a ton of use cases and helpful feedback on how customers wanted to use an extraction model. We heard about use cases ranging from extracting data from images like receipts to reading values from support tickets. We knew that we wanted extraction to be the clear focus for the model, so it had to excel at reading from unstructured data. We decided to go back to the drawing board with Clairic and redesigned our architecture, differentiating this new version of Clairic from our preview release. For ordinary text and number extraction fields, we now use parallel slot autoregressive generation instead of a single forward pass. Each field uses the tokens it has already written to choose its next token, then stops at its own end marker. All the fields advance together in the serving batch, still giving lightning-fast latency per request. This boosted our accuracy in extraction for both text and images, and the trade-off in accuracy offsets the small latency cost. For computation, estimation, and extraction use cases, we trained special heads that can handle estimates, forecasts, durations, calculated dates, and explicit arithmetic. Although the model architecture evolved, we kept the parts of the typed API interface that make the answers useful: confidence scores, character spans, and probabilities are still intact with every request. The model is still incredibly fast and cheap. From the evals below, you can see how our newer versions of Clairic have greatly improved on extraction across text, images, PDFs, and more. There are no public extraction benchmarks yet, but we ran our internal evals for other emerging extraction models on the market, such as Liquid AI’s D1.2 (pipelined with Apple Vision for optical character recognition) and Scaledown’s Extract . items.title: Intent Contracts: Taking Tools Away from Agents
items.summary: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

items.title: Safe Personal RSI: Evaluating and Repairing Personal-Agent Updates
items.summary: Kicker is a personal health assistant. Changes to an assistant's reusable instructions can improve task handling while changing what it discloses, which requests it follows, and how it reports actions. We study Safe Personal RSI, an update-evaluation component developed for Kicker. We restrict recursive self-improvement (RSI) to prompt updates, with model weights and runtime code fixed. The procedure tests proposed and current instructions, repeats failing cases, temporarily undoes changes to guide repairs, and checks safety and task performance before adoption. If no version passes, the current instructions stay in use. Our executable benchmark contains 29 email, calendar, health, and marketplace cases, with separate probes for authorization reuse, memory, and tool-output injection. Across three models and two deliberately risky edits, the procedure rejects 20 of 21 update attempts. In repair confirmation, an admitted GPT-5.6 Luna repair reduces attack violations from 10.7% to 0% and increases safe task completion from 89.7% to 100%; a broad handwritten authority rule matches these outcomes. Under stronger attacks, a repair transferred from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct to Qwen3-14B reduces violations from 69.0% to 17.9% and increases safe task completion from 19.5% to 64.4%. Separate runtime probes examine memory-entry deletion and identify missing local OAuth scope checks in the evaluated snapshot.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.328
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added auto mode for Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude apps gateway; interactive sessions with no permission mode start in it
  • Added "onFailure": "block" for mcp_tool hooks, as for command and HTTP hooks: a hook whose call fails blocks the action
  • Added a warning when a message from a session that skips permission prompts may be held and dropped by a cloud session
  • Added a notice in /status and claude doctor when an OpenTelemetry exporter has no endpoint and its data would likely be lost
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_DEFERRED_TOOL_RESUME, which lets a host stop claude -p --resume and --continue from running a tool call that a hook deferred
  • Added support for apps that embed Claude Code to switch on the policy plugin's allowManagedModsOnly option; an admin's managed settings still win
  • Added a startup warning to the Claude apps gateway when a policy's maxEffortLevel is not a valid effort level
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --repository-folder to name the folder that sessions use for a repository at --capacity 1, in place of its path under the base folder, which can't be a symbolic link
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a start-up warning when the host's settings.json sets a default permission mode that sessions ignore
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --hook-label to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator, to hand chosen session labels to the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --metadata key=value to claude --environment, to label a session for the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_by_reason_seconds to the orchestrator's /metrics, so a re-opened session's wait can be told from a new one's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added an orchestrator metric, claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_sessions_given_up_total, that counts by cause how often Anthropic gave up starting a runner for a session
  • Fixed Bash commands in zsh stopping with a "not found" error at a word that starts with =, such as echo ==== or [ a == b ]; =cmd no longer expands to a command's path
  • Fixed automatic compaction reusing the session's earlier system prompt instead of rebuilding it the way /compact does
  • Fixed markdown rendering freezing on some very long or malformed input
  • Fixed rare screen freezes
  • Fixed Esc often being lost at a permission prompt or question when you typed straight after it; in terminals that send Alt as Esc and a key, an unused Alt or Option key now declines there
  • Fixed a paste or a terminal's reply being typed into the prompt when a slow connection cut it in two
  • Fixed saving a scheduled task erasing the project's other saved tasks when the scheduled tasks file can't be read, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed a scheduled task with a typo in the project's scheduled tasks file being deleted the next time that file was saved
  • Fixed a case where a resumed cloud session could lose its compaction summary or recent messages when a message was saved late
  • Fixed the token counts on the spinner and for subagents counting a retried reply twice, missing replies that were not streamed, and standing still while Claude thinks
  • Fixed the error shown when usage credits run out mid-response, which named a rate limit
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn outside Claude Desktop with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set behind a gateway rejecting betas, on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry or Claude apps gateway
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS not lengthening the 5-minute connection limit on gateways, custom base URLs and cloud providers
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending for good with "Prompt is too long" after large tool results; the largest are now left out
  • Fixed MCP tools whose input schema starts with anyOf, oneOf or allOf going missing on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed an MCP tool with an invalid input schema failing requests on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off; the tool is now left out and Claude is told why
  • Fixed effort being turned off for a subagent's model for the session if Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Foundry refused its progress summary's effort setting (regression in 2.1.327)
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script when a permission prompt outside auto or bypass mode, a plan approval or a question stayed open for ten minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts in auto and bypass-permissions modes failing to call an MCP server that had connected while the previous script was running
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not running in the background in auto or bypass permissions mode in a session chosen in the claude --resume picker
  • Fixed Code Mode losing a loaded skill, hook context or a note typed with a permission approval when resuming a session in which one reply ran several scripts
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a Code Mode script was cut off when the session was resumed from the picker or in a mode that asks for permission
  • Fixed Code Mode silently using undefined for top-level variables that an earlier failed script never set
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not being told when a failing command's long output was cut
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing valid scripts that start with a { block
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing scripts that use both a top-level await and a top-level return
  • Fixed an @-mentioned small file not being attached in Code Mode after a script had read or written it
  • Fixed Code Mode offering write() and edit() to read-only subagents that can't call them
  • Fixed Claude starting a turn by itself in Code Mode when Esc was followed by a command such as /model
  • Fixed Claude in Code Mode not being told to run workflows only when you ask, or the workflow size you set in /config
  • Fixed Remote Control repeating the same disconnect message, and telling you to retry a session that can't reconnect
  • Fixed a waiting permission prompt being lost, and its answer ignored, when a remote session restarted while the service was slow
  • Fixed cloud sessions resuming a cleared conversation after a rewind followed by /clear
  • Fixed a remote session losing a turn's tool calls and results when its runner or worker was lost after a dropped model stream had been retried
  • Fixed cloud and Remote Control sessions that just started, or have an @ in their title, being unreachable in cross-session messaging from a session with Remote Control on
  • Fixed Claude being told that cloud sessions can never reply; it now learns when a reply can come and how else to get the result
  • Fixed /diff, the Changes pane of Remote Control sessions and the diff beside an edit leaving out committed work after a command moved into another repository

  • Fixed Send now in the desktop app and SDK hosts telling Claude that a stopped web search found no results
  • Fixed Cmd+letter being typed into the prompt in terminals that report Cmd
  • Fixed Ctrl+click opening a link twice in GNOME Terminal, side mouse buttons acting as clicks, and the first wheel notch in the other direction being ignored after a pause, in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed Shift+Enter in Konsole outside tmux and ssh, and Alt shortcuts on non-Latin keyboard layouts in terminals that speak the kitty keyboard protocol

  • Fixed text copied in fullscreen mode including the quote bar, losing spaces at line wraps when a drag scrolled upward, or missing words under the "Jump to bottom" pill
  • Fixed an image path pasted into a ! command becoming an attachment
  • Fixed Ctrl+C showing no exit warning while the ? shortcuts list is open
  • Fixed Ctrl+R search in fullscreen mode and the /theme color editor picking the wrong row when keys arrive together, and keys being dropped there and in the search of /config and /plugin
  • Fixed wrong or missing colors inside GNU screen
  • Fixed many background notifications cutting into the top border of open dialogs in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped

  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off

  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number

  • Changed managed PostToolUse hooks to no longer fire for calls refused before they ran: no log entry, rewrite, block or stop there; PostToolBatch gets most, not marked as refused

items.title: Protect sensitive data in your traces: new controls in LangSmith
items.summary: New controls are now in LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data. Learn more.
items.story_key: story|title:protect sensitive data in your traces new controls in langsmith
items.content_excerpt: You can’t run agents in production without governing the data they touch. When that data includes sensitive customer information, controlling access becomes a regulatory and contractual obligation. That puts engineering and security requirements at odds. Engineers need production traces to debug issues and improve agent performance. Security and compliance teams need to enforce least privilege: people should only see the data their job requires. That’s why we’ve added three new controls to LangSmith to help teams manage access to sensitive trace data: Traces give engineers visibility into how an agent behaved and help them identify what needs to improve. When they record production activity, their inputs and outputs often contain sensitive customer data, such as names, health information, or payment details. Companies need to restrict access to this data to meet: First, they can create custom observability setups with duplicate traces and multiple workspaces. Engineers get trace access, but platform teams have more to configure and maintain. The alternative is to avoid sending traces to observability platforms altogether, preventing agent engineers from having visibility and slowing product velocity. We built these new controls so organizations can meet the needs of their engineering and security teams without the messy workarounds. Here’s how it works. You send your traces to LangSmith with full data fidelity, then grant access to only those who need it. Debugging is handled with least privilege, so addressing performance issues like latency can be managed without exposing any sensitive data. If a customer reports an issue, you can grant access to only that customer’s inputs and outputs, and only to the people or teams required to address it. Everything is configurable through granular admin controls. LangSmith’s new input and output controls give admins greater control over what portions of a trace users can see. Trace inputs and outputs are where sensitive user data most often resides. Other trace data like run trees, performance stats, and metadata are critical for agent improvement and far less sensitive. With these controls, agent engineers can spot and resolve issues – like repetitive or slow tool calls – without seeing sensitive content, and those who need the full picture can be granted access as needed. items.summary:
Running one coding agent is easy; running ten that share GitHub, Linear and CI turns software delivery into a distributed systems problem. James Moss, Member of Technical Staff at Tessl, shares five lessons from scaling Tessl's own software factory to 3.5x more merged PRs with the same team: shared state, stale assumptions, convergence, duplicate work, and budgets with stop conditions. Recorded at AI DevCon New York 2026.

What we cover:
– How Tessl's internal software factory grew to handle 85% of PRs
– Why independent tickets don't guarantee independent changes
– Catching stale assumptions when other agents change the code underneath
– Stopping review agents from talking in circles
– Idempotency and fault tolerance for factories built on third-party tools
– Budgets and stop conditions for multi-agent workflows

items.title: Release 2.75.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.11
items.summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • PyTorch backend: Added AOTI BF16 input/output support.
  • THIRD-PARTY-NOTICES.txt is now included in the containers.
  • Fixed a use-after-free in the dynamic batcher and a preserve_ordering completion-slot issue on response-cache hits.
  • Prevented silent gRPC stream cancellations under backpressure.
  • Bounded the decompressed HTTP inference response size in the client library.
  • Perf Analyzer: Honored supplied output shapes, propagated the binary exit code, tagged the wheel as platform-specific, and limited profile-data export to the needed inputs and outputs.
  • Python backend: Now logs when the backend stub exits on a crash signal.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.

items.title: Meta’s Muse: Inside the launch of the most successful consumer product this year | Mona Sarantakos
items.summary:
Muse is the #1 app in the App Store and arguably the fastest-growing AI consumer product of all time. Mona Sarantakos has led product on it since day one. She’s VP of Product at Meta Superintelligence Labs and a 10-year Meta veteran with over 20 years of experience as a PM. This is her first podcast interview.

*We discuss:*
1. How a weekend with OpenClaw on a Raspberry Pi turned into Muse
2. Why Muse waited seven months to launch, despite getting started before most of its competitors
3. How Nat Friedman, Alex Wang, and Mark Zuckerberg each left their imprint on the product
4. How the team uses “agent swarms” to surface user insights at scale
5. The use case nobody on the team predicted
6. How Jolly, a placeholder avatar, became an icon
7. The two levers that actually move activation for an AI agent
8. The #1 thing Mona looks for in PMs today
